raw_transcript:
Okay, recording this in the car in the parking lot, I just finished the onsite, well, the virtual onsite, with Halvard Systems. It's Friday, October 30th, about 4:15. I want to get this down before I forget everything.

So there were four rounds. Four. The recruiter, Sienna Morrow, had said three, but they added a, um, a system design one at the last minute.

Round one, behavioral, with the hiring manager, Gideon Achterberg. He manages the platform reliability team, which is the team I'd be joining. Questions. First was, tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical decision. I used the story about the, the queue migration at my current job, where I pushed back on moving from RabbitMQ to Kafka without a load test, and we ran a load test and found the consumer lag issue. I think that went well. I gave the number, the lag was 45 seconds at peak, and he wrote that down, I saw him writing. Then he asked about a time I failed. And I, ugh, I rambled. I told the story about the missed migration deadline, but I spent too long on the context and didn't get to what I learned until he kind of prompted me. That one was weak. I need to tighten that story. Like, situation in two sentences max.

Round two, coding, with an engineer named Priyanka, uh, Priyanka Venn, I think, Venn. The problem was a rate limiter, implement a sliding window rate limiter. I wrote it in Python, used a deque per client. I got it working, passed her test cases, and then she asked about memory with a million clients and I said we could evict idle clients with, um, with a TTL, but I didn't implement that, we ran out of time. Time complexity, I said amortized O of 1 per request. Wait, I think I said O of log n first, and then corrected myself to amortized O of 1, because the deque pops are amortized. Yeah. Final answer was amortized O of 1. I think it was fine. Not amazing.

Round three, the surprise system design. Design a metrics ingestion pipeline handling 2 million events per second. Honestly, I had not prepared for that specifically. I drew producers, a partitioned log, stream aggregation, and a time series store. The interviewer, Leon Faber, pushed on, on how I'd handle late events, and I said watermarks with a 30 second allowed lateness, and he seemed okay with that. But I completely blanked on the storage sizing. He asked for a rough number of bytes per day and I fumbled the math, I said something like 17 terabytes, then said 170, then I just said I'd need to redo it. That's bad. I should practice back-of-envelope math. The real answer, I just did it now, 2 million per second times 86,400 seconds times say 100 bytes is about 17 terabytes per day raw. So my first number was right and I talked myself out of it. Great. Amazing.

Ugh, also my laptop fan was screaming the whole time, I'm sure they could hear it. I need to clean that thing.

Round four, Gideon again, a short one, mostly about team questions. I asked about on-call, and it's one week in six, and they said they're moving from a home-grown alerting setup to Prometheus and Alertmanager next quarter. I asked about the, um, the level, and Sienna had said senior, Gideon said it's senior but leveling happens after the debrief. So not confirmed.

Compensation, not discussed today. Sienna said she'd call by Wednesday, November 4th with a decision.

Overall, I'd give myself, I don't know, a 6 out of 10. Behavioral strong except the failure story, coding okay, system design shaky on numbers.

Things to do. Send thank-you notes to Gideon, Priyanka, and Leon tonight. I have not sent them yet. Rework the failure story into a STAR format with a tight situation. Do five back-of-envelope estimation problems this weekend. And, um, I have the second round with Corvane Labs on Tuesday the 3rd, so I should prep for that too. Okay. Driving home.

Oh, and actually, I want to note what Leon said at the end, because I think it's useful. He said the strongest part of my design was that I asked about the read pattern before choosing the store, like, whether dashboards query the last hour or the last year, and that most candidates skip that. So that's something to keep doing. And he said the weakest part was I didn't mention backpressure at all, like what happens when the aggregation layer falls behind. I didn't. Totally forgot. So, add that to the checklist: requirements, read patterns, back-of-envelope, backpressure.
